query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Q235 steel’s as‐received state, the inherently formed native oxide layer acts as an effective barrier against corrosion at room temperature but undergoes a phase transformation and spallation under high-temperature (700–900 °C) aggressive salt conditions, leading to accelerated degradation. A pre-annealing treatment that promotes a uniform and adherent oxide scale will mitigate these high-temperature degradation mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received state with a naturally formed, heterogeneous native oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing treatment to intentionally form a uniform, well-adhered oxide layer on Q235 steel, and compare its behavior to untreated samples.
generation.conditions: Corrosion tests conducted at two regimes: room temperature in an aggressive salt solution and high-temperature conditions (700–900 °C) under the same salt exposure. The study should include both as-received and pre-annealed (modified oxide layer) specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: The native oxide scale (or engineered oxide scale produced by annealing) and its integrity (phase composition and adhesion to the substrate).
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the oxide layer remains intact, offering protection by acting as a stable diffusion barrier. However, under high-temperature salt exposure, thermal expansion mismatch or phase transformation of the oxide causes spallation and loss of protective continuity, accelerating corrosion. Pre-annealing is hypothesized to produce a more thermally stable and adherent oxide layer, reducing transformation and spallation under high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, both as-received and annealed samples should show limited corrosion. Under 700–900 °C salt exposure, the as-received samples will experience significant mass loss and visible oxide spallation, whereas the annealed samples will display reduced mass change, improved oxide scale integrity as evidenced by microstructural analysis (e.g., XRD and SEM), and fewer spallation events.
generation.baseline: As-received Q235 steel without any annealing treatment under both temperature regimes.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies only when the aggressive salt composition and exposure conditions are maintained. It does not predict similar outcomes if the salt environment is less aggressive or if exposure temperatures remain within a regime where the native oxide is inherently stable (i.e., room temperature). Additionally, differences in the initial oxide layer composition or unintended surface contaminants may alter the expected behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact phase transformation kinetics, the quantitative threshold of thermal mismatch leading to spallation, and the long-term stability of the engineered oxide layer under cyclic thermal conditions remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set as-received and one set subjected to a controlled annealing treatment to form a uniform oxide layer. Expose both sets to an aggressive salt solution at room temperature and at high temperatures (700–900 °C) for equal durations. Characterize the mass loss, oxide scale integrity (using XRD and SEM), and occurrence of spallation events.
measurements: Phase composition and crystallinity of the oxide layer (XRD)
Adhesion quality of the oxide scale (possibly via scratch tests or cross-sectional imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature exposed annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in corrosion performance (i.e., similar mass loss, oxide spallation, and phase transformation) compared to as-received samples, or if both sample types perform similarly at room temperature, the hypothesis that oxide scale integrity governs the differential corrosion behavior across temperature regimes would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

The grain size is quite large, on the order of hundreds of micrometers and elemental EDS mapping revealed that the material is compositionally homogeneous and devoid of segregation as shown in Fig. 2 . Limited porosity was observed in the microstructure, possibly due to oxygen impurities from the precursor material, solidification shrinkage, or Kirkendall voiding during homogenization treatment [18] . The XRD pattern shown in Fig. 3 confirmed the alloy to be single phase, polycrystalline material with FCC crystal structure.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on high-temperature corrosion in advanced alloys (including HEAs and stainless steels) have largely focused on performance metrics such as hardness, wear resistance, and mass change during salt exposure. They typically compared alloyed systems with engineered processing (annealing, casting, surface modification) but did not isolate the fundamental role of the pre‐existing oxide state in dictating corrosion behavior across different temperatures. For instance, in PMC6908586, accelerated elemental dissolution and oxide scale evolution were observed in HEAs vs. stainless steel during molten salt exposure at 700 °C, suggesting that variations in oxide scale composition and integrity directly affect corrosion performance. However, such studies did not address whether the inherent oxide layer on an as‐received material (here, Q235 steel) is intrinsically protective at room temperature yet prone to degradation (via phase transformation, spallation, or thermal mismatch) at elevated temperatures.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved whether the corrosion protection in Q235 steel’s pre‐exposure state is governed by an intrinsic, well‐adhered passive oxide layer that works effectively at room temperature, but which may transform (losing adhesion or changing phase composition) under 700–900 °C salt exposure, leading to accelerated degradation. The specific mechanism by which oxide scale integrity (or its failure) controls the transition between protective and degradative behavior across temperature regimes has not been isolated.
decision.lever: Pre-forming or modifying the native oxide layer (via a controlled annealing treatment) on Q235 steel to produce a uniform, adherent oxide versus leaving the as‐received state unchanged, followed by parallel corrosion tests at room temperature and at 700–900 °C under aggressive salt exposure.
decision.why: This approach directly isolates the effect of the pre-existing oxide scale on corrosion behavior. It builds on the trend seen in earlier studies where engineered modifications (such as post-annealing in HEAs or stainless steels) impacted oxide evolution and corrosion performance. By comparing an annealed (modified oxide) sample with an untreated reference, the study can test the hypothesis that oxide integrity governs corrosion protection at room temperature but fails (e.g., through spallation or phase change) at high temperatures, with specific observations (e.g., changes in mass loss, oxide composition via XRD/SEM, and spallation events) serving both as support and potential falsification of the hypothesis.
